items.title: Quantum algorithms for multidimensional partial differential equations
items.subtitle: Quantum linear-algebra methods for scientific PDE workloads
items.summary: Research on quantum and hybrid quantum-classical methods for solving multidimensional PDEs, including circuit-efficient formulations, practical case studies, and singular-value-based approaches for scientific workloads.
overview: This research explores how quantum linear-algebra techniques can be used to formulate and solve multidimensional partial differential equations that arise across scientific and engineering applications.
The work emphasizes practical circuit structure, scalability, and validation across representative PDE families rather than treating the quantum algorithm as an isolated mathematical primitive.

sections.heading: Research direction
paragraphs: The central question is how to map structured PDE problems into quantum computations while keeping the circuit construction efficient enough to study on simulators and available hardware.

Recent work extends this direction toward quantum singular-value decomposition and transformation and hybrid quantum-classical workflows for computational fluid dynamics and nuclear-physics equations.

items.title: Particle Track Reconstruction
items.subtitle: High-performance C++ reconstruction with helical estimation, interchangeable search, parallel conflict resolution, and reproducible validation
items.summary: A clean-room C++ particle-tracking system that treats reconstruction as both an estimation problem and a systems problem. The current automatic pipeline reconstructs all 500 reference tracks in the controlled TrackML validation subset while preserving modular search, parallel execution, geometry-aware recovery, and reproducible quality checks.
items.visualAlt: Transverse detector view showing hundreds of measured TrackML particle trajectories radiating from the collision region.
items.visualCaption: Transverse view of the controlled 500-track TrackML validation subset from event000001000, generated from measured hit coordinates.
overview: Particle Track Reconstruction is a native C++ research platform for studying the full tracking problem: forming track hypotheses from detector hits, propagating and fitting those hypotheses, resolving shared-hit conflicts, recovering incomplete trajectories, and validating both physics quality and computational performance.

The implementation combines helical EKF reconstruction with structure-of-arrays data layouts, automatic front-end hypothesis generation, multiple bounded search strategies, collaborative hit handling, geometry-aware trajectory completion, packed binary input, truth matching, and reproducible benchmark and release tooling.

sections.heading: Reconstruction system
paragraphs: The project is designed as a complete reconstruction engine rather than a single algorithm experiment. Its canonical path begins with detector hits and carries candidate tracks through hypothesis formation, filtering and branching, global conflict handling, optional refinement, and trajectory completion.

The architecture keeps the numerical tracking core separate from search policy, data movement, collaboration, and validation so each part can be studied without turning the codebase into a one-off benchmark.
items: Helical EKF propagation, gating, update, refit, residual, and pull analysis
Structure-of-arrays event and candidate storage with packed .ptrkbin input
Automatic, region, displaced, adaptive, ensemble, and fusion hypothesis-generation paths
Geometry-aware trajectory completion and incomplete-track recovery
Collaborative hit handling, global conflict resolution, and deterministic matching
Native C API plus CLI, benchmark, matrix, and release-validation executables

sections.heading: Current validation
paragraphs: The current merged default is validated on a fixed public TrackML subset built from event000001000: the 500 highest-pT charged particles with pT at least 0.5 GeV, |eta| at most 2.5, and at least four recorded hits. The selected workload contains 5,605 measured hits.

Starting from the measured hits, the automatic pipeline reconstructs all 500 reference tracks on this controlled subset and returns exactly 500 reconstructed tracks, with zero fake tracks and zero duplicate tracks. The configured native test suite passes 34 of 34 tests, and all four disjoint 250-track robustness windows from the same public event close at 100% seed recall and 100% reconstruction efficiency. Across those windows, fake rate spans 0.38–1.49% and duplicate rate spans 1.94–5.22%. These measurements are scoped validation results, not a claim of perfect reconstruction for arbitrary detectors or occupancies.

sections.heading: Search and estimation
paragraphs: The reconstruction problem is exposed through interchangeable brancher policies instead of being hard-wired to one search heuristic. The engine supports deterministic EKF candidate building alongside bounded A*, ant-colony, particle-swarm, simulated-annealing, and Hungarian-style strategies.

This makes the codebase useful for studying where tracking quality comes from: the state estimator, the candidate-search policy, the hit-assignment objective, or the global conflict solver. Search budgets and quality controls remain bounded so comparisons can be reproduced.

sections.heading: Parallel and data-oriented implementation
paragraphs: The systems side of the project focuses on keeping useful physics work dominant over bookkeeping. Dense hit IDs can use compact lookup structures, candidate data uses structure-of-arrays layouts, immutable geometry information is reused across iterations, and collaboration work can adapt to the measured conflict signal.

Thread sweeps, release gates, stability checks, backend policies, and parity tooling are part of the repository so performance changes can be evaluated together with efficiency, fake rate, duplicate rate, and reconstruction stability rather than as isolated timing numbers.

sections.heading: Research questions
items: How should local track-state estimation and global hit assignment be coupled?
Which search policies give the best quality-compute tradeoff under bounded candidate growth?
How much collaboration between tracks is useful before synchronization and conflict bookkeeping dominate?
Which data layouts and geometry caches preserve reconstruction quality while improving CPU efficiency?
How should throughput claims be scoped so candidate-building, automatic front-end work, and full reconstruction are not conflated?

sections.heading: Validation scope
paragraphs: The 100% figure is end-to-end automatic reconstruction efficiency on the fixed 500-track validation subset. The front-end seed diagnostic also reaches 100% recall on this subset, with 99.085% purity; seed diagnostics remain supporting evidence rather than the focus of the project.

The repository also contains tooling for controlled comparisons with mkFit and for multi-window or multi-event quality matrices when additional TrackML events are available. The public project description does not treat older stage-matched timing runs as current evidence. Different events, detector geometries, occupancies, hardware, and experiment-specific reconstruction chains require their own validation.
